                                          PROJECT NO. 58000

    EVALUATION OF TRANSMISSION                          §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
          COST RECOVERY                                 §                OF TEXAS
                                                        §
                                                        §

          COMMENTS OF BASE POWER COMPANY ON STAFF’S RECOMMENDED

      PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDMENTS TO §25.192 AND §25.193.


    I.​    INTRODUCTION
Base Power Company (“Base”) submits these comments in response to the Commission Staff’s
proposed rule for publication in the above-referenced project. Base Power uses this opportunity
to reiterate the comments and points made in Retail Electric Providers for Affordable, Innovative
Rates (“REPAIR’s”) response to Staff’s Draft Report1.

Base continues to urge the Commission to consider the inequity in market participation
opportunities between large industrial users and the entirety of the residential customer class. It
has been Base’s position that while the imposition of demand charges and a change in the
number or duration of Coincident Peaks (“CPs”) may very well be appropriate, it is an
inadequate solution on its own if the Commission’s goal, as directed by the Governor and
Legislature, is to substantially reduce transmission costs for residential consumers. Base does not
oppose the move from 4CP to 12CP, the codification of a 30-minute measurement interval,
annual updates to class allocation factor values, or the minimum billing demand provisions for
large load customers. However, what the proposed rule does not address, and what Base
respectfully submits the Commission must address, is the structural asymmetry in the retail
transmission billing framework that will persist regardless of how many coincident peaks the
Commission adopts.




1
 Retail Electric Providers for Affordable, Innovative Rates Comments on Commission Staff Report Filed Jointly by
Base Power Company, Octopus Energy, Rhythm Energy, and Tesla Energy Ventures, LLC, 58484-82
https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/search/documents/?controlNumber=58484&itemNumber=82
     II.​   CHANGING THE NUMBER OF COINCIDENT PEAKS DOES NOT CHANGE
           WHO CAN RESPOND TO THEM
The proposed rule appropriately reforms the upstream transmission cost allocation methodology.
It does not, however, reform the downstream billing structure through which those costs are
ultimately passed to residential customers served by Retail Electric Providers ("REPs"). This
distinction matters enormously.

Under the current billing framework, which the proposed rule leaves intact, REPs are billed for
the transmission costs attributable to their residential customers on a flat per-kilowatt-hour
(“kWh”) basis. There is no demand-based signal in this billing structure. A REP that successfully
reduces its residential customers' peak demand during coincident peak intervals receives no
financial benefit for doing so. The cost savings flow elsewhere.

The consequence is a staggering disparity in the incentive to engage in demand response. A
transmission-connected large load customer that reduces one megawatt of demand during
coincident peak intervals saves approximately $68,550 per year under current Oncor tariff rates.
A REP that reduces the same amount of demand on behalf of its residential customers saves
approximately $94 per year, a 727-to-1 difference, for the same action on the same grid.2

Moving from 4CP to 12CP does not correct this disparity. The proposed rule changes how many
peak intervals are counted in the upstream allocation. It does not change the fact that residential
REP customers have no structural mechanism to benefit from reducing demand at any of those
intervals. The asymmetry is not a function of the number of coincident peaks. It is a function of
the retail billing design, which this rulemaking does not touch.

ERCOT data shows that 44.6% of residential customers in Non-Opt-In Entity ("NOIE") territory
are enrolled in demand response programs, compared to only 10.1% of residential customers in
REP territory.3 NOIEs face demand-based transmission cost exposure directly, on behalf of all
their customers. That exposure gives them a powerful financial incentive to invest in demand
response infrastructure including their residential customers. REPs have no equivalent incentive.


2
  5 OnCor Electric Delivery TCRF Rider (January 2026). Transmission-connected large load: full postage-stamp rate
x 1 MW = $68,550/yr (727x vs. residential REP). Commercial/industrial demand-based: $3.395/kW-mo x 12 =
$40,740/yr (432 x). Residential REP flat-rate equivalent: -$94/yr per MW (lx baseline). PUCT Dkt. 57491 (2025
TCOS).
3
  2024 Annual Report on Demand Response in the ERCOT Region.
 The enrollment gap reflects a difference in market structure, not in customer capability or
program design.



III.​    A COMPLEMENTARY RETAIL BILLING REFORM IS NECESSARY TO
         FULFILL SENATE BILL 6'S MANDATE
Senate Bill 6 charged the Commission to evaluate whether the Commission's retail ratemaking
practices ensure that transmission cost recovery appropriately charges the system costs caused by
each customer class. That mandate is not satisfied by reforming only the upstream allocation if
the downstream billing structure continues to deny the residential class any meaningful
opportunity to respond to, and reduce, the costs that the upstream methodology assigns to them.

Base Power and its REPAIR co-filers previously proposed a straightforward, complementary
reform: allow REPs to elect demand-based transmission billing on a portfolio basis, consistent
with how commercial and industrial ("C&I") customers are billed today. Under this proposal:

    ●​ A REP electing demand-based treatment would receive invoices from its Distribution
         Service Provider ("DSP") for transmission charges calculated on the basis of the REP's
         actual coincident-peak load contribution, in the same manner as transmission-connected
         large load customers.
    ●​ The election would be portfolio-wide for the REP within a given DSP territory, and
         would be implemented through the annual allocation factor update proceeding that the
         proposed rule already establishes under amended § 25.193.
    ●​ The electing REP would be required to intermediate the demand-based charge on behalf
         of its residential customers. It could not pass through a demand charge directly to end-use
         residential customers. This protection has precedent in other restructured retail markets in
         the United States.4
    ●​ The proposal is revenue-neutral for DSPs and Transmission Service Providers ("TSPs").
         It changes only who bears the financial responsibility for managing a defined portion of
         coincident-peak load, not the total transmission costs collected system-wide.


4
 See, for example, the Pennsylvania PUC's "fixed means fixed" regulation, codified at 66 Pa.C. S. §2807(d), which
as interpreted has prevented the pass-through of demand charges that are inconsistent with the pricing of Provider of
Last Resort rate design.
 This reform would, for the first time, give residential customers served by REPs the same
structural opportunity to reduce their transmission costs through demand response that C&I and
NOIE customers have long had. It would create a financial incentive for REPs to invest in smart
thermostats, batteries, time-of-use pricing, and other demand-reducing technologies on behalf of
their customers.



IV.​   REQUEST
Base Power asks the Commission to take one of two actions. First, and preferably, the
Commission should direct that the opt-in demand-based billing election described in REPAIR's
Project No. 58484 comments be incorporated into the final rule in this proceeding, using the
annual allocation factor update mechanism established by amended § 25.193 as the vehicle for
implementation.

Alternatively, the Commission should make clear in the adopting order for this rulemaking that
the residential billing asymmetry identified in these comments, and in REPAIR's comments in
Project No. 58484, remains an open item for priority resolution, and should initiate a successor
proceeding or direct Staff to develop an implementation proposal on a defined schedule.



                                                                        Respectfully submitted,




                                                                   _______________________


                                                    ​      ​       ​      ​      Tori Villarreal
                                                                          Base Power Company
                 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY — BASE POWER COMPANY

                                    PROJECT NO. 58000



Base Power Company respectfully submits the following summary of the substantive points
made in these comments:



          ●​ Base Power does not oppose the proposed rule, including the shift from 4CP to
             12CP, the 30-minute measurement interval, annual allocation factor updates, and
             the minimum billing demand provisions for large load customers.
          ●​ Base Power takes no position on Staff's specific questions regarding the structure
             or duration of the large load minimum billing demand provisions.
          ●​ The proposed rule reforms the upstream transmission cost allocation methodology
             but leaves intact the downstream retail billing structure, under which REPs are
             billed for residential transmission costs on a flat per-kWh basis with no
             demand-based component.
          ●​ This billing structure produces a 727-to-1 disparity in the financial incentive to
             reduce coincident-peak demand: a large load customer saves approximately
             $68,550 per year per megawatt reduced, while a REP acting on behalf of
             residential customers saves approximately $94. Moving from 4CP to 12CP does
             not correct this disparity.
          ●​ Base Power, as part of the REPAIR coalition, previously proposed a
             complementary reform in Project No. 58484: allow REPs to opt in to
             demand-based transmission billing on a portfolio basis, implemented through the
             annual allocation factor update proceeding under amended §25.193,
             revenue-neutral to DSPs and TSPs, with electing REPs required to intermediate
             the demand charge rather than passing it through directly to residential customers.
          ●​ Base Power asks the Commission either to incorporate this opt-in mechanism into
             the final rule in this proceeding, or to direct that a successor proceeding be
             initiated on a defined schedule to address the residential billing asymmetry as a
             priority matter.
